info.name: openplan API
info.description:
Every route in docs/openapi.yaml, generated by scripts/postman-collection.
Do not edit it in Postman: run `make postman-collection` after changing the spec.

Setup:
1. Select the "openplan local" environment.
2. Sign in at the web UI, then copy the openplan_session cookie's value into
   session_cookie. Keep it in the current value, which stays on your machine.
3. Run the collection top to bottom. Each create request saves the id the
   next one needs, and the asynchronous ones (a registration, a plan) are
   polled until they finish.

Every response is checked for a request id, and every JSON error for the
{error, message, request_id} envelope. "Sign out" revokes the session, so it
runs last.

Templates
item.description: Registering Terraform sources as immutable, reusable revisions.

request.description:
Points openplan at a GitHub repository and a revision, and starts an
asynchronous registration: resolve the ref to a commit, fetch the
source, and infer the root module's input variables.

Returns `202` with a registration record, not a revision. Poll
`GET /v1/tenants/{tenant_id}/template-registrations/{registration_id}`
until its `status` is terminal; on `completed` it carries the
`template_revision_id` the rest of the API takes.

Poll this after `POST /v1/tenants/{tenant_id}/template-revisions`.

In a collection run this re-sends itself until the registration ends, and saves its revision.

The variables inferred from the revision's Terraform root module. A
revision is immutable, so this answer never changes for a given id.

This is the schema a stack template's `config` is validated against.

item.name: Stacks
item.description: Grouping installed templates into one environment or service.

request.description:
Synchronous. The stack row, the audit event and the authorization edges
that make the stack reachable are written in one transaction, so a
`201` response describes a stack that is already usable and a failure
leaves no stack behind. There is nothing to poll.

Only the stacks the caller may view. Each carries its
`effective_capabilities`, so a client renders the controls a person
actually has rather than probing for them.

Plans waiting for approval and destroys that failed, on every stack
the caller may view: waiting plans first, then failed destroys, each
newest first. Viewing a stack is enough to see its items; approving
is checked when someone approves.

item.name: Read a stack with its installed templates
Install a template revision into a stack

request.description:
`config` is validated against the revision's variables, so register the
revision and read its variables first.

The config is empty, which suits a template whose variables all have defaults, as the demo template does. Fill it in for one that has required variables.

item.name: Edit an installed template's desired config

request.description:
Replaces the desired config wholesale — this is not a field-level
merge. The new config is validated against the desired revision's
variables.

Refused with `409 run_in_flight` while the component has an unfinished
run, a plan waiting for approval included: a run snapshots the config
when it starts, and the plan being reviewed has to stay a plan of what
the component says. Apply or discard the run first.

item.name: Stage an installed template on a newer revision

request.description:
Moves the component's *desired* revision. Nothing is applied here —
upgrading is a deliberate, reviewable step, so the new revision takes
effect only when a subsequent apply succeeds. Until then
`desired_template_revision_id` and `last_applied_template_revision_id`
differ and `live_state` reads `differs`.

Omit `config` to carry the current one forward; supply it when the new
revision's variables changed.

item.name: Credentials
item.description: Write-only cloud credentials, injected only while Terraform runs.

request.description:
Credentials are write-only. The value is encrypted on the way in and is
never readable back through the API — it is injected into the process
environment only while Terraform runs. To change one, delete it and
create it again.

`name` is the provider environment variable name, such as
`AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`.
Metadata only. Values are never returned.

Same write-only contract as a stack credential, scoped to one installed
component. Use this to override a stack-wide credential for a single
component.
Metadata only. Values are never returned.

item.name: Runs
item.description: Starting, watching, approving and discarding Terraform operations.

request.description:
Runs are durably orchestrated: a plan or apply survives a process
restart rather than being lost halfway.

Operations work the way the Terraform CLI's do. `plan` only plans the
desired config: the run records what would change and completes,
keeping no plan. `apply` plans the desired config and saves the plan;
`destroy` plans the destruction of everything the component manages
and saves that. For either, a plan with no changes completes the run,
and a plan with changes waits in `waiting_approval`, where approving it
applies exactly that saved plan (see the approval endpoint).

`auto_approve` is allowed on `apply` only. The run then applies
straight away, with no saved plan and nothing to approve, and records
the counts the apply reports. It takes approve permission on the stack
as well as operate permission.

One component runs one operation at a time, and a plan waiting for
approval counts. Starting a second while one is in flight returns `409
run_in_flight` — the competing run is visible through the list
endpoint, so a client can wait for it, or approve or discard it.

An apply, so that its plan waits for approval and the approval request has something to approve.

response.name: 409 runInFlight
409 planStale

request.description: Most recent first.

Poll this to follow a run. `status` moves through the `TemplateRunStatus` values.

In a collection run this re-sends itself until the plan has finished.

Metadata for each Terraform command that has finished, in the order
they ran: the plan's logs, then the apply's, each by `seq` — not the
output itself. Fetch a body from the per-log endpoint by its `phase`.

Returns the raw Terraform output as `text/plain`, not JSON. A phase
that has not produced output yet returns `404`.

item.name: Approve a waiting plan, which applies it

request.description:
Valid only while the run's `status` is `waiting_approval`. Approving
starts the apply of the plan the run saved: the same file, applied
with `tofu apply` on whichever executor picks it up, so what was
reviewed is exactly what runs. If the state has moved on since the
plan was made, tofu refuses the plan and the run fails; plan again.

Refused with `409 plan_stale` if the plan no longer describes the
component's desired config and revision. Those cannot change while
the plan waits, so this is a backstop.

Takes no fields: send `{}` or no body at all.

`409` when the plan had no changes, so there is nothing to approve.

item.name: Discard a plan waiting for approval

request.description:
Throws away a run's saved plan while it waits for approval (or is
approved and not yet applying). The run ends `canceled` straight away
and its plan can never be applied. A run that is planning or applying
cannot be stopped.

The body is optional: send no body to discard without a reason.

Discards the approved plan if its apply has not started yet; `409` once it has.

item.name: Users
item.description: Searching people who have signed in at least once.

item.name: Search people who have signed in

request.description:
Matches display name or email, case-insensitively.

This is not a directory lookup. It searches openplan's projection of
identities it has actually verified, so a person who has never signed
in will not appear — and cannot be granted a role. That is the same
limitation `POST .../grants` enforces as `unknown_user`.

The response echoes the `first` and `max` actually applied, so a client
paginates from what the server used rather than from what it sent.

Saves the first match who is not you, for the grant requests.

item.name: List role grants on a stack
Assign a role on a stack

request.description:
Assigning replaces whatever role the subject already held — one person
has at most one role on a stack.

The subject must have signed in to openplan at least once. openplan is not
a directory: a person exists here only once a verified token has
projected them. Granting to a subject it has never seen returns `400
unknown_user`. Use `GET /v1/tenants/{tenant_id}/users/search` to find
one.

The response is the intended grant, rendered from the identity
lookup the request already performed. The authorization write
itself is queued and reconciled asynchronously, so a permission
check made immediately afterwards may still answer from the old
state.

Needs a second person who has signed in once; without one there is nobody to grant a role to.

item.name: List the caller's queued work items

request.description:
The asynchronous work the caller queued — template registration,
template runs. Scoped by actor alone, so no new permission concept is
involved: a caller only ever sees their own items. Capped at the 50
most recent.

item.description: Signing in and out. The only routes reachable without a session.

exec: // Sent without a session, as a browser reaches this route.

query.description:
Where to send the browser after a successful sign-in. Validated as
a same-site path; anything else falls back to the site root.

request.description:
Redirects the browser to the identity provider's authorization
endpoint. Makes no network call of its own: the endpoint comes from
discovery the verifier already cached. Sets a short-lived sealed
transaction cookie (`openplan_auth_tx`) carrying state, nonce and PKCE
verifier.

exec: // Sent without a session, as a browser reaches this route.
pm.test('failure is the HTML sign-in page', () => pm.expect(pm.response.headers.get('Content-Type')).to.include('text/html'));

query.description: Compared in constant time against the sealed transaction cookie.

request.description:
Redeems the authorization code on the back channel, verifies the ID
token and its nonce, and hands the browser a session cookie. Redirects
rather than rendering, so the authorization code leaves the address bar
and the browser history.

Every failure renders one identical page. Distinguishing "bad state"
from "expired code" from "nonce mismatch" would tell an attacker which
check they tripped.

Only the identity provider can complete a sign-in, with a real code and the transaction cookie. Sent from here it shows the one failure page every cause gets.

Revokes the session row and clears the cookie, then sends the browser
on to end the provider's session. Revoking the row rather than only
clearing the cookie is what makes logout real: a copy of the cookie
taken beforehand stops working too.

The redirect carries the raw ID token as `id_token_hint`, which is how
RP-initiated logout is specified and what stops the provider
interrupting with a confirmation page. A provider that advertises no
end-session endpoint — Dex, today — gets the site root instead. Dex
v2.45.1 keeps no browser session, so nothing of the sign-in outlives
openplan's session except an upstream connector's own.

Revokes the session `session_cookie` holds, so it runs last.

item.name: Accept an OIDC back-channel logout token

exec: // Sent without a session, as a browser reaches this route.

request.description:
A server-to-server POST from Dex, not a redirect the browser follows.
Dex v2.45.1 never calls it; a Dex release with browser sessions does,
once the client registers it as `backchannelLogoutURI`. The address
must be one Dex can reach — on the Compose stack
`http://api:8081/v1/auth/backchannel-logout`, not `OPENPLAN_PUBLIC_URL`.

It ends openplan sessions as soon as the Dex session behind them ends,
instead of at their own expiry — openplan stops consulting Dex once a
session exists.

The body is capped at 64 KiB.

Only the identity provider can send a valid logout token. A forged one is refused.
